paras: The 1919 Millen race riot was an outbreak of violence near Millen, Georgia, on April 13, 1919, that began when two white officers arrested a Black man at a church gathering and left both officers and at least four Black men dead. Afterward a white mob burned Black churches, lodge halls and automobiles, and Black papers reported at least one further Black man lynched. Black editors treated the episode as an attack on prosperous Black farmers.

The gathering was held at a rural Black church that the Chicago Broad Ax and the New York Age called Buckhead Church and the Chicago Defender placed at Carlsruhe Grove. According to a Washington Bee correspondent who met eyewitnesses in Augusta the next day, the uniformed Knights of Pythias had gathered for a sermon and Joe Ruffin, one of the wealthiest Black farmers in the county, was marshal of the day.

A wire dispatch dated Millen, April 13, said County Policeman W. C. Brown and Night Marshal T. H. Stephens went to the church on a report that liquor was being distributed. They stopped Edmond Scott in an automobile with a Black preacher and arrested him on a charge of carrying a concealed weapon. In this account Joe Ruffin was alleged to have opened fire, and both officers, Ruffin's three sons and Scott were killed.

The Bee's correspondent said the officers found no liquor but handcuffed a man holding an "unconcealed gun," and when Joe Ruffin offered to go his bond, Stephens shot Ruffin in the head. Ruffin's son Louis, recently discharged from the army, then shot Stephens dead, and the prisoner ("some say by an officer"), the other officer and one Ruffin son were killed.

A special report from Millen said a Black man was taken from the jail and lynched and that seven Black lodge and church buildings were burned. The Bee described a white mob of "hundreds" that burned churches, automobiles and halls and killed a young Ruffin son "for the crime of being one of the family."

A traveler told the Chicago Defender that more than 400 Black families in the area were leaving for the Northwest. No report of an inquest or trial appears in the coverage, and the man said to have been lynched is not named. In May the Savannah Tribune listed Millen among Georgia towns marked by mob "slaughtering and burning."

The Richmond Planet printed the April 13 wire as "Six Die in Duel," under a headline reading "Colored Officers Open Fire on Colored Men," although other reports identified the officers as white. The Associated Negro Press redistributed it under an April 24 dateline to the Dallas Express and the St. Louis Argus, and none of these versions questioned the allegation that Ruffin fired first.

The Broad Ax and the New York Age ran the Millen special on April 19, the Age as a front-page "Extra!" headlined "Whites Burn Church Building in Georgia" that called the lynched man "innocent." The Defender's brief item, datelined "Milton, Ga.," said the officers "were not justified in interfering with the meeting."

In Georgia the Savannah Tribune called the episode "The Jenkins County Murders" and traced it to envy of Black farmers who owned automobiles. A week later it rebuked the Augusta Chronicle and the Macon Telegraph, which it said had used the "Jenkins county tragedies" to criticize Black leaders. The fullest Black account came at the end of May from the Bee's correspondent, "T. W.," who answered Florida governor Catts's claim that only the "worthless" Black man was lynched. He wrote that the white press stressed the Ruffins' wealth, including Joe Ruffin's "high power car," as if it were one of their offenses.

The wire alleged that Ruffin fired first; the Bee, citing eyewitnesses, said Stephens did, and only the Bee names its sources. The Black dead also differ by report: Scott and three Ruffin sons in the wire, Ruffin and three sons in the A.N.P. version, and Scott, "John Ruffin" and two brothers in the Gazette. The Defender named only Scott and "another onlooker," the Millen special added the man lynched from jail, and the Bee said Joe Ruffin survived and was jailed at Augusta.

reader.title: 1919 Millen race riot
bases: Two white officers' arrest of a Black man at a church gathering ended in a gunfight, after which a white mob burned Black churches, lodges and cars and reportedly lynched one or more Black men [A5][A1][A16].

The gunfight deaths were not mob killings, but the Millen special reports a Black man 'taken from the jail and lynched' [A1][A3] and the Bee says a white mob of hundreds killed a young Ruffin son out of vengeance [A16]; the two reports disagree on the victim.

The shooting at the church with six dead is reported independently by the wire, the Gazette, the Savannah Tribune and the Bee, and the arson and a mob killing by both the Millen special and the Bee [A5][A11][A6][A1][A16].

accounts.label: Wire report (later A.N.P.)
accounts.gist: Officers answering a liquor report arrested Scott for a concealed weapon; it is alleged Joe Ruffin opened fire; both officers, Ruffin's three sons and Scott killed; Stephens's body claimed beaten by the crowd.

accounts.label: Millen special
accounts.gist: Seven dead in race riots at Buckhead Church, including a Black man taken from jail and lynched; seven Black lodge and church buildings burned.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender
accounts.gist: Officers tried to break up a revival at Carlsruhe Grove and were killed; Scott and another onlooker shot; the officers were not justified.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Washington Bee, from eyewitnesses)
accounts.gist: Officers found no liquor, arrested a man with an unconcealed gun, and Stephens shot Joe Ruffin when he offered bond; Louis Ruffin killed Stephens; a white mob then burned churches and killed a young Ruffin son.

framing.detail: Richmond Planet 'Six Die in Duel', A.N.P. reprints and the Gazette brief carry the wire's allegation that Ruffin fired first without comment.
New York Age 'Extra! Whites Burn Church Building in Georgia', calling the lynched man 'innocent'.
Defender: officers 'were not justified in interfering with the meeting'; reports an exodus.
Savannah Tribune editorials: 'The Jenkins County Murders', rooted in envy of thrifty Black automobile owners; rebuts the Augusta Chronicle and Macon Telegraph.
Washington Bee 'Race Riots at Millen, Ga.: A Close-Up' blames the officers and the mob and the white press's stress on Ruffin's wealth.

versions.value: Officer Stephens shot Ruffin, then Louis Ruffin shot Stephens

conflicts.note: The Bee's version rests on eyewitnesses its correspondent met the next day; the wire's is unsourced ('it is alleged').

sources.note: 'White Officer Is Killed', dateline Milton, Ga., April 18, printed inside a New York heart-balm suit story: officers tried to break up a revival at Carlsruhe Grove; Scott and another onlooker shot; 400 families leaving.
quotes: As far as could be learned the police officers were not justified in interfering with the meeting.

sources.note: 'Extra! Whites Burn Church Building in Georgia', Millen, Monday: same seven-dead text as the Broad Ax, riot begun 'Sunday'; 'one innocent Negro' taken from jail and lynched.
quotes: One innocent Negro was taken from jail and lynched.

sources.note: Headline 'Colored Officers Open Fire on Colored Men at Millen, Ga' and opening of the April 13 wire dispatch: six killed in a pistol battle 'this afternoon'.
quotes: Six persons were killed in a pistol battle between county officers and colored men near here this afternoon

sources.note: 'Six Die in Duel', continuation of the wire: Scott arrested for a concealed weapon; liquor report; alleged Joe Ruffin opened fire; officers, Ruffin's three sons and Scott killed; Stephens's body claimed beaten.
quotes: Other colored men intervened and it is alleged Joe Ruffin opened fire on the officers.
After Stephens had been shot it is claimed his head and body were beaten by the crowd of colored men.

sources.note: Editorial 'The Jenkins County Murders': six died 'last Sunday'; blames envy of thrifty Negroes who owned pleasure automobiles.
quotes: a deep seated envy and animosity toward a few thrifty and industrious Negroes there

sources.note: Associated Negro Press version of the wire, dateline 'Milton, Ga., April 24', badly garbled; Ruffin and three sons killed.
Editorial answering the Augusta Chronicle and Macon Telegraph, which drew on the 'Jenkins county tragedies' to criticize Negro leaders.
quotes: These two newspapers, two of the most powerful in the state and south, have sounded a very hopeless note for the future peace and prosperity of the southland.

sources.note: A.N.P. wire, 'Millen, Ga., April 24': same account as the Planet; Scott met in an automobile with the minister; 'Later Ruffin and his three sons were killed.'

'Doings of the Race' brief: six killed in a riot in northern Jenkins County April 13; names the dead as officers C. B. Brown and Stephens (white), Scott, John Ruffin and two Ruffin brothers (colored).
Editorial on Southern lawlessness quoting a justification from 'the Jenkins county lynching'; the victim's name is left blank.
quotes: the people decided to take the law into their own hands and bring matters to a close.

sources.note: Editorial continuation listing Millen among Georgia towns marked by mob 'slaughtering and burning'; announces NAACP meeting at St. Philip church.
'Race Riots at Millen, Ga.: A Close-Up', signed T. W.: writer reached Augusta April 14 and met eyewitnesses; Knights of Pythias gathering at a rural church; Joe Ruffin marshal of the day.

Bee continuation: officers found no liquor, arrested a man with an 'unconcealed gun'; Stephens shot Ruffin when he offered bond; Louis Ruffin killed Stephens; Joe Ruffin survived and was jailed at Augusta.
quotes: The "bad-tempered" man simply replied with his gun, the bullet hitting Ruffin in the head and dropping him in his car.
